pharm: Fluoroquinolone; inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase & topoisomerase IV
quick: Ophthalmic 0.5%: 1 drop q2h day 1 (up to 8x), then 2-4x/day days 2-7
Ophthalmic: not applicable; oral (non-US): with or without food
Ophthalmic: no human data, low systemic exposure; oral: avoid
Ophthalmic: low systemic levels, likely compatible; oral: caution
Ophthalmic: no adjustment; oral (non-US): reduce if CrCl <40
Ophthalmic: allergy/superinfection; oral: blood glucose, QT, tendons
summary: Gatifloxacin is an 8-methoxyfluoroquinolone. The ophthalmic solution 0.5% (Zymaxid) is FDA-approved for bacterial conjunctivitis and is the only current FDA-approved form. The oral/systemic form (Tequin) was voluntarily withdrawn from the US market in 2006 by Bristol-Myers Squibb due to serious dysglycemia (both hypo- and hyperglycemia) and is not FDA-approved, though it remains marketed in some countries (e.g., India); systemic data here are flagged as pending clinical review.
indications: Bacterial conjunctivitis caused by susceptible organisms (ophthalmic 0.5% — FDA-approved)
Oral/systemic respiratory and urinary infections (historical Tequin use; NOT FDA-approved — withdrawn 2006; pending review)

dosage.d: Day 1: 1 drop in affected eye(s) every 2 hours while awake, up to 8 times
dosage.n: FDA-approved (Zymaxid). For topical ophthalmic use only; do not inject.

dosage.d: Days 2-7: 1 drop in affected eye(s) 2 to 4 times daily while awake
dosage.n: Effective and safe in patients >=1 year; not established below 1 year.
WITHDRAWN in US (2006) for serious dysglycemia; NOT FDA-approved; pending clinical review. Carries fluoroquinolone class risks. Still marketed in some countries.

admin: Ophthalmic: wash hands; tilt head back and instill drop into conjunctival sac of affected eye(s)
Ophthalmic: do not let dropper tip touch the eye, fingers or any surface to avoid contamination
Ophthalmic: if using other eye drops, separate by at least 5 minutes
Ophthalmic: for topical ocular use only — never inject into the eye or use intracamerally (risk of corneal endothelial injury)
Oral (non-US, historical): take with or without food; separate from antacids/iron/zinc/multivitamins by >=2 hours; maintain hydration
moa: Bactericidal fluoroquinolone that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, enzymes essential for bacterial DNA replication, transcription, repair and recombination. The 8-methoxy structure broadens gram-positive and anaerobic activity. No cross-resistance with aminoglycosides, macrolides or tetracyclines.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to gatifloxacin, to other quinolones, or to any component of the formulation
relative: Diabetes mellitus or glucose dysregulation — systemic gatifloxacin caused severe dysglycemia (basis for US withdrawal)
History of myasthenia gravis (systemic fluoroquinolones may worsen muscle weakness)
Known QT prolongation, uncorrected hypokalemia, or concomitant QT-prolonging drugs (systemic use)
History of tendon disorders or prior fluoroquinolone-associated serious reaction (systemic use)
monitor: Ophthalmic: signs of hypersensitivity (rash, swelling) and superinfection with prolonged use
Systemic: blood glucose (both hypo- and hyperglycemia)
Systemic: tendon pain/swelling, QT, CNS effects and peripheral neuropathy

preg: Ophthalmic: no adequate human data; systemic exposure after topical ocular use is very low (serum below 5 ng/mL limit of quantification). Oral animal data show teratogenicity at doses far above the human ophthalmic dose. Systemic use is not FDA-approved — avoid.
lact: Ophthalmic: no human milk data, but systemic levels after ocular use are very low; likely compatible with care. Gatifloxacin appears in rat milk after oral dosing; for systemic use, weigh benefit vs infant risk.
renal: Ophthalmic: no adjustment needed (negligible systemic absorption). Oral/systemic (non-US, historical): dose reduction recommended in significant renal impairment (e.g., CrCl <40 mL/min) — not FDA-approved.
hepatic: No specific ophthalmic dosage adjustment. Systemic use not FDA-approved; data pending review.

major: Systemic only — Antidiabetic agents (insulin, sulfonylureas): severe hypo- and hyperglycemia; primary reason oral form was withdrawn
Systemic only — QT-prolonging drugs (class IA/III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, antipsychotics, TCAs): additive torsades risk
Systemic only — Corticosteroids: increased tendon rupture risk
moderate: Systemic only — Multivalent cations (antacids, iron, zinc, sucralfate, multivitamins): reduced oral absorption
Systemic only — NSAIDs: may increase CNS stimulation/seizure risk
Ophthalmic: minimal systemic interaction potential due to low absorption
interactions.food: Ophthalmic: not applicable. Oral (non-US): may be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Ophthalmic: not relevant. Systemic: avoid; may add to CNS effects.
interactions.diagnostics: Class fluoroquinolones may cause false-positive opiate urine screens with systemic use; topical ophthalmic use unlikely to interfere.

serious: Hypersensitivity/anaphylactic reactions and angioedema (may occur after a single dose)
Growth of resistant organisms/superinfection (including fungi) with prolonged use
Corneal endothelial cell injury if introduced into the anterior chamber
Systemic: severe dysglycemia (life-threatening hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia)
Systemic: QT prolongation / torsades de pointes
rare: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (reported with topical ophthalmic use)
emergency: Anaphylaxis or serious skin reaction (may occur after first dose) — seek emergency care
Systemic: severe hypoglycemia (confusion, loss of consciousness) or marked hyperglycemia in diabetics
Systemic: sudden severe chest, back or abdominal pain (possible aortic dissection)
Systemic: tendon pain/snap/swelling — stop drug and seek care
Systemic: new numbness/tingling/weakness, seizures or severe mood changes

monitoring: Ophthalmic: signs of allergic reaction (rash, itching, swelling, dyspnea) — discontinue if they occur
Ophthalmic: superinfection with prolonged use; examine with slit lamp/fluorescein when indicated
Systemic: blood glucose closely (both hypo- and hyperglycemia)
Systemic: tendon symptoms (especially >60 yrs, on steroids, transplant patients)
Systemic: ECG/QT in at-risk patients; CNS and peripheral neuropathy symptoms
counsel: Ophthalmic: do not touch the dropper tip to your eye or any surface — keep it sterile
Ophthalmic: complete the full 7-day course even if the eye looks better
Ophthalmic: stop and contact your doctor at the first sign of rash, swelling or hypersensitivity
Ophthalmic: remove contact lenses while you have conjunctivitis and during treatment
Oral form is not FDA-approved and was withdrawn in the US in 2006 for serious blood-sugar effects
If a systemic gatifloxacin product is used abroad: diabetics must monitor blood sugar and watch for low- and high-sugar symptoms
Systemic use: report tendon pain, numbness/tingling, or mood/seizure changes immediately
pk: Ophthalmic: local action at site; systemic absorption negligible
Ophthalmic: serum levels below limit of quantification (<5 ng/mL); oral Tmax ~1-2 h
Systemic ~7-14 hours (oral); minimal systemic exposure after ocular use
Ophthalmic: dosed up to 8x on day 1, then 2-4x/day; oral once-daily
Store at 15-25 C (59-77 F); protect from freezing
pearls: ORAL/SYSTEMIC GATIFLOXACIN (Tequin) IS NOT FDA-APPROVED — voluntarily withdrawn from the US market in 2006 (Bristol-Myers Squibb) for serious dysglycemia; systemic content here is pending clinical review
Only the ophthalmic 0.5% solution (Zymaxid) is FDA-approved (bacterial conjunctivitis) and is the current recommended use
Systemic gatifloxacin caused both severe hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, with disproportionate risk in elderly and diabetic patients — avoid systemically in diabetes
As a fluoroquinolone, systemic use carries class risks: tendinitis/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, QT prolongation, aortic aneurysm/dissection, and worsening of myasthenia gravis
Zymaxid is for topical ocular use only — introduction into the anterior chamber can cause corneal endothelial cell injury
Rare Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and anaphylaxis (even after a single dose) have been reported with topical ophthalmic gatifloxacin
Oral gatifloxacin remains marketed in some countries (e.g., India) despite US withdrawal
missed: Ophthalmic: instill the missed drop as soon as remembered; if near the next dose, skip it and resume the schedule. Do not double up. (Oral form not FDA-approved.)
overdose: Ophthalmic overdose is unlikely to cause systemic toxicity given negligible absorption; flush the eye with warm water if excess instilled. Systemic overdose (non-US): supportive care, hydration, ECG/glucose monitoring; not efficiently removed by dialysis.
